The hexagonal lattice is universally locally optimal

Thomas Leblé ††thanks: Université de Paris-Cité, CNRS, MAP5 UMR 8145, F-75006 Paris, France thomas.leble@math.cnrs.fr
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We prove that the hexagonal lattice is a local minimizer, among all point configurations, of the interaction energy per unit volume for pair potentials that are completely monotonic functions of the square distance. This includes Gaussian interactions and power laws.

Dedicated to Sylvia Serfaty on the occasion of her 50t​h50^{th} birthday.

1 Introduction

When f:(0,+∞)→ℝf:(0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R} is a function, and 𝖷⊂ℝ2\mathsf{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is a locally finite collection of points, define the ff-energy

Ef​(𝖷):=lim infr→∞1|𝖷∩Br|​∑x,y∈𝖷∩Br,x≠yf⁡(|x−y|),\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{X}):=\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|\mathsf{X}\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in\mathsf{X}\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}f(|x-y|), (1.1)

where Br\mathrm{B}_{r} is the disk of center 00 and radius rr, while |𝖷∩Br||\mathsf{X}\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}| is the number of points in Br\mathrm{B}_{r}.

The goal of this paper is to prove that if ff is of the form f:r↦e−π​α​r2f:r\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}, or f:r↦r−sf:r\mapsto r^{-s}, then the hexagonal lattice 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is a local minimizer of Ef\mathrm{E}_{f} among point configurations. Our result extends to all completely monotonic functions of the square distance, see Section 1.2.

An important conjecture states that 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is in fact the global minimizer of those energies at fixed density. However, we are not aware of any local minimality result.

1.1 The hexagonal lattice

We denote by 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} the hexagonal lattice 𝖠2:=σ​ℤ+τ​ℤ\mathsf{A}_{2}:=\sigma\mathbb{Z}+\tau\mathbb{Z}, seen as a collection of points in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, where:

σ:=r⋆×(1,0),τ:=r⋆×(12,32),r⋆:=23.\sigma:=r_{\star}\times(1,0),\quad\tau:=r_{\star}\times\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right),\quad r_{\star}:=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}.

The quantity r⋆r_{\star} is the minimal distance between lattice points. A fundamental domain ℋ\mathcal{H} of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is given by the Voronoi cell of the origin, i.e. the set of points which are closer to the origin than to any other lattice point, see Figure 1. With our choice of r⋆r_{\star}, the area of ℋ\mathcal{H} (the “covolume”) is equal to 11.

In this paper, “local” is understood with respect to small, bounded perturbations of the lattice: take 𝐩:𝖠2→ℝ2\mathbf{p}:\mathsf{A}_{2}\to\mathbb{R}^{2}, and consider the perturbed lattice obtained by shifting each lattice point xx by 𝐩⁡(x)\mathbf{p}(x):

𝖠2+𝐩:={x+𝐩⁡(x),x∈𝖠2}.\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}:=\{x+\mathbf{p}(x),\ x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\}.

We define the size of a perturbation 𝐩\mathbf{p} as

‖𝐩‖:=supx∈𝖠2|𝐩⁡(x)|.\|\mathbf{p}\|:=\sup_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}|\mathbf{p}(x)|.

Whenever ‖𝐩‖\|\mathbf{p}\| is finite, the resulting point configuration 𝖠2+𝐩\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p} has density 11, in the sense that

limr→∞1|Br|​|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br|=1.\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\left|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}\right|=1. (1.2)

In order to ensure that 𝖠2+𝐩\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p} remains simple, and to shorten some computations, we assume that:

‖𝐩‖≤120​r⋆.\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{20}r_{\star}. (1.3)

Since we are aiming at local results, this is not restrictive. We often write 𝐩x\mathbf{p}_{x} instead of 𝐩⁡(x)\mathbf{p}(x).

1.2 Main results

For α>0\alpha>0, denote by Φα\Phi_{\alpha} the Gaussian interaction potential Φα:r↦e−π​α​r2\Phi_{\alpha}:r\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha r^{2}}. Our first result is:

Theorem 1.

For all α>0\alpha>0, there exists ε\varepsilon (depending on α\alpha) such that:

If ‖𝐩‖≤ε\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, then EΦα​(𝖠2+𝐩)≥EΦα​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{\Phi_{\alpha}}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{\Phi_{\alpha}}(\mathsf{A}_{2}). (1.4)

The value of ε\varepsilon can be chosen uniformly for α\alpha in compact subsets of (0,+∞)(0,+\infty).

Following [CK07], there is a strong interest in considering more general interaction potentials ff that are completely monotonic functions of square distance (we call them here “c.m.s.d”). Recall that a smooth function gg is completely monotonic when (−1)k​g(k)≥0(-1)^{k}g^{(k)}\geq 0 for all k≥0k\geq 0. A c.m.s.d function is then defined as being of the form f⁡(r)=g⁡(r2)f(r)=g(r^{2}), where gg is completely monotonic. It follows from a theorem of Bernstein that every c.m.s.d function ff can be written as a mixture of Gaussians, i.e. there exists a certain positive measure Wf\mathrm{W}_{f} on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty) such that for all r>0r>0, the following integral is finite and:

∫0+∞Φα​(r)​𝚍​Wf​(α)=f⁡(r).\int_{0}^{+\infty}\Phi_{\alpha}(r)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)=f(r). (1.5)
Theorem 2.

Let ff be a c.m.s.d function. There exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 (depending on ff) such that:

If ‖𝐩‖≤ε\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, then Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)≥Ef​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}). (1.6)

More generally, let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of c.m.s.d. functions, and assume that the following condition is satisfied:

limα0→0,α1→∞∫α1+∞e−π​α2​r⋆2​𝚍​Wf​(α)+∫0α0α−1​𝚍​Wf​(α)∫1+∞e−π​α​r⋆2​𝚍​Wf​(α)+∫01e−πα​r⋆2​𝚍​Wf​(α)=0​ uniformly for f∈ℱ.\lim_{\alpha_{0}\to 0,\alpha_{1}\to\infty}\frac{\displaystyle{\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{\alpha_{0}}\alpha^{-1}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)}}{\displaystyle{\int_{1}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)+\int_{0}^{1}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)}}=0\text{ uniformly for $f\in\mathcal{F}$.} (1.7)

Then 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is uniformly locally optimal for f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}, namely there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that:

If ‖𝐩‖≤ε\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon, then Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)≥Ef​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) for all f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F}.
Remark 1.1.

When writing (1.6), we implicitly assume Ef​(𝖠2)<+∞\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2})<+\infty, which, for a c.m.s.d function ff, is equivalent to r↦r​f​(r)r\mapsto rf(r) being integrable at infinity, or to α↦α−1\alpha\mapsto\alpha^{-1} being Wf\mathrm{W}_{f}-integrable at 00, see (3.53). Otherwise, it is easy to see that both sides of (1.6) are +∞+\infty.

The power-law (or Riesz) potentials fs:r→r−sf_{s}:r\to r^{-s} are c.m.s.d functions whose measure Ws\mathrm{W}_{s} has density:

𝚍​Ws𝚍​α=πs2​αs2−1Γ⁡(s2).\frac{\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{s}}{\mathtt{d}\alpha}=\frac{\pi^{\frac{s}{2}}\alpha^{\frac{s}{2}-1}}{\Gamma(\frac{s}{2})}. (1.8)

As a direct application of Theorem 2, we obtain that 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is locally optimal for every fsf_{s}, and that ε\varepsilon can be chosen uniformly for ss in compact subsets of (2,+∞)(2,+\infty) (when s≤2s\leq 2, the interaction energies are infinite).

1.3 Connection with the literature and the “universal optimality” conjecture

The lattice 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is famously optimal with respect to circle packing. It is moreover known, or expected, to solve many other optimization problems, see [Gru00]. This is an instance of “crystallization”, namely the observation that, in various settings, optimal point configurations exhibit a regular structure, see [BL15].

In that regard, a major open problem consists in proving that 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is “universally optimal” for energy minimization, i.e. is a global minimizer, among point configurations of density 11 in the sense of (1.2), of every Gaussian interaction energy, see [CK07, Conjecture 9.4] - such interactions are sometimes referred to as the Gaussian core model in the physics literature [Sti76]. By Bernstein’s theorem, this would imply global minimality for every c.m.s.d interaction potential. Partial results are few:

  • •

    In [Mon88], Montgomery proved that 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} minimizes all those energies among lattices. This result has later been generalized in many directions, see e.g. [SS12, Theorem 2] for an extension to the Coulomb energy, or [BF23] and references therein for variations on the topic of minimization among lattices.

  • •

    Some recent results have gone slightly beyond the lattice case, for instance [HT25] shows universal optimality of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} among point configurations with a period of 44 or 66 points.

  • •

    A proof of local optimality among all periodic configurations - with an implicit dependency on the period - had been given in [CS12], but a flaw was unfortunately later found by the authors [CS22].

  • •

    As put in [FSZ24] “the status of universal optimality of the hexagonal lattice has been set back to the result of Montgomery from 1988”.

In this paper, we prove local minimality of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} for all c.m.s.d functions, together with a quantitative understanding, in terms of ff, of:

  1. 1.

    The size ε\varepsilon of the neighborhood around 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} on which we guarantee local minimality of Ef​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}).

  2. 2.

    A lower bound, in terms of 𝐩\mathbf{p}, on Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Ef​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) when ‖𝐩‖≤ε\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon.

Moreover, we obtain a form of “local universal optimality”, as we show that ε\varepsilon can be chosen uniformly for reasonable families of c.m.s.d functions, see Theorem 2. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results of this kind. However, it is fair to say that:

  • •

    We remain far from the full conjecture, both qualitatively and quantitatively (our ε\varepsilon’s are very small).

  • •

    The techniques are local by nature and cannot possibly yield a global result.

Remark 1.2.

In dimension 88 and 2424, both sphere packing and universal optimality were recently solved thanks to major breakthroughs by Viazovska et al. We refer to [CKM+22, Sec. 1] for an introduction to such problems and a survey of what is known, or expected, in other dimensions.

1.4 Plan of the paper

Since c.m.s.d functions are mixtures of the Φα\Phi_{\alpha}’s, most of the work is devoted to proving, in a quantitative way, that 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is locally optimal with respect to Gaussian interactions.

  • •

    In Section 2, we introduce some important tools and lemmas. In particular:

    • –

      We show that it is enough to consider periodic perturbations (Lemma 2.1).

    • –

      We present a “periodic” version of the 22-design property for regular hexagons (Proposition 2.9).

    • –

      We state a key minimality result for a certain lattice sum (Proposition 2.12).

  • •

    In Section 3, we prove a quantitative version of Theorem 1, then use it to deduce Theorem 2.

  • •

    An appendix is devoted to the proof of auxiliary results. In particular, Appendix C, which takes up a significant portion of the paper, consists in proving the minimality result of Proposition 2.12.

Acknowledgements. We thank Sylvia Serfaty for introducing us to such topics quite some time ago. We thank Martin Huesmann for initial discussions, and Antoine Tilloy for his help with positivity questions.

2 Preliminaries

We denote the inner product of two vectors x,yx,y of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} by x⋅yx\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}y.

2.1 Convention for Fourier analysis on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}

Fourier transforms.

We define the Fourier transform φ^\hat{\varphi} of a Schwartz function φ\varphi as:

φ^:k↦φ^(k):=∫ℝ2φ(x)e−2iπx⋅k𝚍x.\hat{\varphi}:k\mapsto\hat{\varphi}(k):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\varphi(x)e^{-2i\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}\mathtt{d}x.

With this convention, the Gaussian11 1 𝖦α\mathsf{G}_{\alpha} is a function ℝ2→ℝ\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} whereas in Section 1.2, the function Φα\Phi_{\alpha} is [0,+∞)→ℝ[0,+\infty)\to\mathbb{R}. We have 𝖦α​(x)=Φα​(|x|)\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}(x)=\Phi_{\alpha}(|x|). family 𝖦α:x↦e−π​α​|x|2\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}:x\mapsto e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}} on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} satisfies

𝖦α^=α−1​𝖦α−1​ for α>0.\widehat{\mathsf{G}_{\alpha}}=\alpha^{-1}\mathsf{G}_{\alpha^{-1}}\text{ for $\alpha>0$.} (2.1)
Reciprocal lattice and Pontryagin dual.

We denote by 𝖠^2\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} the reciprocal lattice of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}, defined as:

𝖠^2:={k∈ℝ2,k⋅x∈ℤ for all x∈𝖠2}.\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}:=\left\{k\in\mathbb{R}^{2},\ k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}x\in\mathbb{Z}\text{ for all }x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\right\}.

In practice 𝖠^2\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} corresponds to applying a rotation of angle π2\frac{\pi}{2} to 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}. We denote by Ω\Omega the fundamental domain of 𝖠^2\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} obtained by applying the same rotation to ℋ\mathcal{H}.

The Pontryagin dual of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is the torus ℝ2/𝖠^2\mathbb{R}^{2}/\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}, which can be identified with Ω\Omega.

Poisson summation formula.

If φ:ℝ2→ℝ\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} is a Schwartz function and u∈ℝ2u\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we have:

∑x∈𝖠2φ⁡(x+u)=∑k∈𝖠^2φ^​(k)​e2​i​π​k⋅u.\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}\varphi(x+u)=\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}\hat{\varphi}(k)e^{2i\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}.

2.2 Periodic functions and Fourier transforms.

We will use sub-lattices of the form N​𝖠2:=N​σ​ℤ+N​τ​ℤN\mathsf{A}_{2}:=N\sigma\mathbb{Z}+N\tau\mathbb{Z} for some integer N≥1N\geq 1, where σ,τ\sigma,\tau are the basis vectors of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}. The reciprocal lattice of N​𝖠2N\mathsf{A}_{2} is given by

N​𝖠2^=1N​𝖠^2.\widehat{N\mathsf{A}_{2}}=\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}.

We say that a function gg defined on 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} is N​𝖠2N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic if

g⁡(x+y)=g⁡(x)​ for all x∈𝖠2 and all y∈N​𝖠2.g(x+y)=g(x)\text{ for all $x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}$ and all $y\in N\mathsf{A}_{2}$}. (2.2)

Equivalently22 2 We will abuse notation and not distinguish between gg and the corresponding map on the quotient space., gg can be seen as function on the discrete torus 𝖠2/N​𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}. When gg is N​𝖠2N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic, we define its Fourier transform as the following function, defined for “frequencies” kk in 1N​𝖠^2/𝖠2⋆\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}:

g^:=k↦1N2∑x′∈𝖠2/N​𝖠2g(x′)e−2iπk⋅x′.\hat{g}:=k\mapsto\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}g(x^{\prime})e^{-2i\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}x^{\prime}}. (2.3)

Then the Plancherel identity holds:

1N2​∑x′∈𝖠2/N​𝖠2|g⁡(x′)|2=∑k∈1N​𝖠^2/𝖠^2|g^​(k)|2.\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}|g(x^{\prime})|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}|\hat{g}(k)|^{2}. (2.4)

We refer e.g. to the lecture notes [Tao07] for a pedagogical presentation of this topic.

2.3 Reduction to periodic perturbations

Lemma 2.1.

Let ff be a c.m.s.d function. Let 𝐩\mathbf{p} be a perturbation such that ‖𝐩‖<+∞\|\mathbf{p}\|<+\infty, and let δ>0\delta>0. There exists N≥1N\geq 1 and a perturbation 𝐩per\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}} which is N​𝖠2N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic in the sense of (2.2), such that:

  1. 1.

    The size of perturbations does not increase: ‖𝐩per‖≤‖𝐩‖\|\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}}\|\leq\|\mathbf{p}\|.

  2. 2.

    The corresponding ff-energy increases by at most δ\delta:

    Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩per)≤Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)+δ.\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\leq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})+\delta.

The proof of Lemma 2.1 is elementary, we postpone it to Section A. In order to prove local minimality results, it is thus enough to study periodic perturbations - provided that our analysis does not depend on the size of the period.

2.4 Properties of periodic perturbations

Let 𝖫\mathsf{L} be a sub-lattice of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}, let 𝖠2/𝖫\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L} be the quotient set, which is finite, and let 𝐩\mathbf{p} be a 𝖫\mathsf{L}-periodic perturbation. For x∈𝖠2x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, we define Qx\mathrm{Q}_{x} as the following probability measure on ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}:

Qx:=1|𝖠2/𝖫|​∑x′∈𝖠2/𝖫δ𝐩x′+x−𝐩x′.\mathrm{Q}_{x}:=\frac{1}{|\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}}\delta_{\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+x}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}}. (2.5)

This object is crucial for us. It encodes the distribution of “relative displacements” in the direction xx.

Remark 2.2.

Since x′↦x′+xmod𝖫x^{\prime}\mapsto x^{\prime}+x\mod\mathsf{L} is a permutation of 𝖠2/𝖫\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}, the measure Qx\mathrm{Q}_{x} is always centered:

∑x′∈𝖠2/𝖫𝐩x′+x−𝐩x′=0.\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}}\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+x}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}=0.

Energy of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} plus periodic perturbations.

For α>0\alpha>0, denote by Eα​(𝖷)\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{X}) the Φα\Phi_{\alpha}-energy of a point configuration 𝖷\mathsf{X} in the sense of (1.1).

Lemma 2.3.

If 𝐩\mathbf{p} is a periodic perturbation, we have:

Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)=∑x∈𝖠2,x≠0∫ℝ2Φα​(|x+u|)​𝚍​Qx​(u).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},x\neq 0}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|x+u|\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u). (2.6)

In particular,

Eα​(𝖠2)=∑x∈𝖠2,x≠0Φα​(|x|).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},x\neq 0}\Phi_{\alpha}\left(|x|\right).
Proof.

This is essentially [CK07, Lemma 9.1], which states33 3 Their Λ\Lambda is our 𝖫\mathsf{L}, their NN is our |𝖠2/𝖫||\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}|, and their points vv corresponds to our perturbed lattice points x+𝐩xx+\mathbf{p}_{x}. Their sum runs over x∈𝖫x\in\mathsf{L} such that x+x′−x′′+𝐩x′−𝐩x′′≠0x+x^{\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}+\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime\prime}}\neq 0. Probabilistic formulation.

If 𝐩\mathbf{p} is 𝖫\mathsf{L}-periodic for some sub-lattice 𝖫\mathsf{L}, let 𝐩∙\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}} be the random family of vectors defined by:

𝐩∙:=(𝐩x+x∙)x∈𝖠2,\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}:=(\mathbf{p}_{x+x^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}})_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}, (2.7)

where x∙x^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}} is chosen uniformly at random in the period 𝖠2/𝖫\mathsf{A}_{2}/\mathsf{L}. It is 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}-stationary in the sense that:

For all z∈𝖠2z\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, (𝐩x∙)x∈𝖠2\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}\right)_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}} and (𝐩x+z∙)x∈𝖠2\left(\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x+z}\right)_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}} have the same finite-dimensional distributions. (2.8)

With this point of view, the measure Qx\mathrm{Q}_{x} defined in (2.5) represents the law of 𝐩x∙−𝐩0∙\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}. In particular:

∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qx​(u)=𝔼⁡[|𝐩x∙−𝐩0∙|2].\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{x}-\mathbf{p}^{\mathbin{\scalebox{.5}{$\bullet$}}}_{0}\right|^{2}\right]. (2.9)

is positive semi-definite. This has important “spectral” consequences, as we present next.

2.6 Spectral measure(s)

Denote by 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+} the cone of symmetric positive 2×22\times 2 matrices with real coefficients. A 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued measure is a map defined on the Borel σ\sigma-algebra of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, with values in 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}, satisfying the natural requirements (σ\sigma-additivity etc.) for being a measure, see [Kim11, Sec. 1.2 & 1.3].

Existence of the spectral measure.

The following result generalizes Bochner’s theorem on Fourier transforms of positive-definite functions.

Lemma 2.4 ([Fal69]).

There exists a 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued measure 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}}, defined on the Pontryagin dual Ω\Omega, such that:

Rx=∫Ωcos⁡(2​π​x⋅ω)​𝑑𝖱^​(ω)​ for all ​x∈𝖠2.\mathrm{R}_{x}=\int_{\Omega}\cos\left(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega\right)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\text{ for all }x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}. (2.13)

The measure 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}} is called the spectral measure of the perturbations. For a pedagogical presentation, building on the classical theorem of Bochner, we refer to [Kim11, Thm. 2.2.3]. We sketch the argument:

Proof.

Both x↦Rx11x\mapsto\mathrm{R}^{11}_{x} and x↦Rx22x\mapsto\mathrm{R}^{22}_{x} are positive-definite (real-valued) functions in the usual sense, so by Bochner’s theorem their Fourier transform is a finite positive measure on the Pontryagin dual Ω\Omega. As for x↦Rx12=Rx21x\mapsto\mathrm{R}^{12}_{x}=\mathrm{R}^{21}_{x}, it is not positive-definite in general, but can easily be written as the difference of two positive-definite functions, thus its Fourier transform is a (signed) measure on Ω\Omega, with finite total mass. It remains to check that those four measures put together define a 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}-valued measure 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}}. ∎

Remark 2.5.

The general result is stated in the Hermitian case, however here R\mathrm{R} is real-symmetric, and Rx=R−x\mathrm{R}_{x}=\mathrm{R}_{-x} by stationarity, thus Rxa​b=∫Ωcos⁡(2​π​x⋅ω)​𝚍​𝖱^a​b​(ω)\mathrm{R}_{x}^{ab}=\int_{\Omega}\cos(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}(\omega) and Rx=∫Ωcos⁡(2​π​x⋅ω)​𝑑𝖱^​(ω)\mathrm{R}_{x}=\int_{\Omega}\cos(2\pi x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\omega)\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega).

The trace measure and trace derivative.

Let 𝖱^a​b\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} (a,b∈{1,2}a,b\in\{1,2\}) be the components of 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}}, which are (real-valued) finite measures on Ω\Omega, corresponding to the Fourier transform of the components of R\mathrm{R}. Define the (real-valued) “trace” measure τ​𝖱^\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}} as:

τ​𝖱^:=𝖱^11+𝖱^22,\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}:=\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{11}+\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{22}, (2.14)

which is positive and finite, because so are 𝖱^11\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{11} and 𝖱^22\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{22}. Since 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}} takes values in 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+}, we know that for all a,b∈{1,2}a,b\in\{1,2\}, the measure 𝖱^a​b\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} is absolutely continuous with respect to τ​𝖱^\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}. Define the “trace derivative” 𝖱^′\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime} as the matrix-valued measurable map ω↦𝖱^′​(ω)\omega\mapsto\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}(\omega), defined on Ω\Omega, such that:

𝖱^′:=𝚍​𝖱^𝚍​τ​𝖱^​ in the sense that ​(𝖱^′)a​b=𝚍​𝖱^a​b𝚍​τ​𝖱^​ for a,b∈{1,2}.\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}:=\frac{\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}}{\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}}\text{ in the sense that }\left(\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}\right)^{ab}=\frac{\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}}{\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}}\text{ for $a,b\in\{1,2\}$.}

It follows from [Ros64] that for τ​𝖱^\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}-a.e. ω\omega in Ω\Omega, the matrix 𝖱^′​(ω)\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}(\omega) is in 𝖲2+\mathsf{S}_{2}^{+} and can be diagonalized44 4 The choice of v1,v2,λ1,λ2v_{1},v_{2},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2} can be made in a measurable fashion [Wil72]. in some orthonormal basis (v1​(ω),v2​(ω))(v_{1}(\omega),v_{2}(\omega)), with eigenvalues λ1​(ω),λ2​(ω)\lambda_{1}(\omega),\lambda_{2}(\omega) such that

λ1​(ω)+λ2​(ω)=1.\lambda_{1}(\omega)+\lambda_{2}(\omega)=1.

If f=(f1,f2):Ω→ℝ2f=(f_{1},f_{2}):\Omega\to\mathbb{R}^{2} is bounded, we can write:

∑a,b∈{1,2}∫Ωfa​fb​𝚍​𝖱^a​b=∫Ω(f⋅𝖱^′​f)​𝑑τ​𝖱^=∫Ω(λ1​(f⋅v1)2+λ2​(f⋅v2)2)​𝑑τ​𝖱^.\sum_{a,b\in\{1,2\}}\int_{\Omega}f_{a}f_{b}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab}=\int_{\Omega}\left(f\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{\prime}f\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}=\int_{\Omega}\left(\lambda_{1}(f\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{1})^{2}+\lambda_{2}(f\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v_{2})^{2}\right)\mathtt{d}\tau\widehat{\mathsf{R}}. (2.15)
Lemma 2.6.

We have for all x∈𝖠2x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}:

∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qx​(u)≤8​π2​|x|2​𝚝𝚛​(∫Ω|ω|2​𝑑𝖱^​(ω)).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\leq 8\pi^{2}|x|^{2}\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|\omega|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right).

(2.16)

∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qx​(u)=2​𝚝𝚛​(R0−Rx)≤8​π2​|x|2​𝚝𝚛​(∫Ω|ω|2​𝑑𝖱^​(ω)).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)=2\mathtt{tr}(\mathrm{R}_{0}-\mathrm{R}_{x})\leq 8\pi^{2}|x|^{2}\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|\omega|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right). (2.17)

2.7 A “periodic 22-design” inequality

Regular hexagons are 22-designs.

Each non-zero lattice point is part of a “shell” of six distinct lattice points, obtained by applying a rotation of angle k​π3\frac{k\pi}{3} (k=0,…,5k=0,\dots,5), which form the vertices of a regular hexagon. Regular hexagons enjoy a certain geometric property known as being a 22-design.

Definition 2.7.

[CS12, Lemma 4.3] Let SS be a finite set of points on the circle of radius r>0r>0, assume that SS is symmetric around the origin. It is said to be a spherical 22-design when for all u∈ℝ2u\in\mathbb{R}^{2}, we have:

1|S|​∑s∈S(s⋅u)2=12​r2​|u|2.\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}|u|^{2}. (2.18)

The right-hand side of (2.18) is what one would obtain by averaging s↦(s⋅u)2s\mapsto(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2} over the circle r​𝕊1r\mathbb{S}^{1} of radius rr, in other words we have the equality:

1|S|​∑s∈S(s⋅u)2=12​π​r​∫s∈r​𝕊1(s⋅u)2​𝑑s.\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{s\in r\mathbb{S}^{1}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\mathtt{d}s. (2.19)
Remark 2.8 (Regular hexagons are 55-designs).

For a regular hexagon of sidelength rr, one can in fact replace the power 22 in (2.19) by any power up to 55. Equivalently (see [CS12, Definition 4.2 & Lemma 4.3]), for any polynomial P:ℝ2→ℝ\mathrm{P}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to\mathbb{R} of total degree up to 55, we have:

1|S|​∑s∈SP⁡(s)=12​π​r​∫s∈r​𝕊1P⁡(s)​𝑑s.\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{s\in S}\mathrm{P}(s)=\frac{1}{2\pi r}\int_{s\in r\mathbb{S}^{1}}\mathrm{P}(s)\mathtt{d}s.
A periodic 22-design inequality.

If SS is a “shell” of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} as described above, and (Qx)x∈𝖠2(\mathrm{Q}_{x})_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}} are the measures associated to a periodic perturbation as in (2.5), can we ensure that, for some 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0:

∑s∈S∫ℝ2(s⋅u)2​𝚍​Qs​(u)≥𝚌​∑s∈S∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qs​(u)​?\sum_{s\in S}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{s}(u)\geq\mathtt{c}\sum_{s\in S}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{s}(u)\ ? (2.20)

If we had Qs=Q\mathrm{Q}_{s}=\mathrm{Q} for some Q\mathrm{Q} independent on ss, we could exchange the sum and the integral and write:

∑s∈S∫ℝ2(s⋅u)2​𝚍​Qs​(u)=∫ℝ2(∑s∈S(s⋅u)2)​𝑑Q​(u)=12​r2×|S|×∫ℝ2|u|2​𝑑Q​(u),\sum_{s\in S}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{s}(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\sum_{s\in S}(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u)^{2}\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}(u)=\frac{1}{2}r^{2}\times|S|\times\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}(u),

using the 22-design property (2.18), which would yield (2.20). The problem55 5 This is, in essence, one of the breaking points in [CS12], see their erratum [CS22]. is that Qs\mathrm{Q}_{s} does depend on ss.

The next proposition shows that, by averaging over a period, one recovers a certain inequality reminiscent of the 22-design property. For a regular hexagon, we sometimes say “radius” instead of sidelength.

Proposition 2.9 (Periodic 22-design inequality).

Let SS be a shell of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} of radius r>0r>0. Let 𝐩\mathbf{p} be a perturbation which is N​𝖠2N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic for some N≥1N\geq 1, in the sense of (2.2). We have:

∑s∈S∑x′∈𝖠2/N​𝖠2|s⋅(𝐩s+x′−𝐩x′)|2≥14​r2​∑s∈S∑x′∈𝖠2/N​𝖠2|𝐩s+x′−𝐩x′|2.\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}(\mathbf{p}_{s+x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}r^{2}\sum_{s\in S}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|\mathbf{p}_{s+x^{\prime}}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}\right|^{2}. (2.21)

Using our definition (2.5) of the measures (Qx)x∈𝖠2(\mathrm{Q}_{x})_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}, the inequality (2.21) (divided by N2N^{2}) yields (2.20) with 𝚌=14​r2\mathtt{c}=\frac{1}{4}r^{2}. The proof of Proposition 2.9 relies on the following geometric lemma:

Lemma 2.10.

Let SS be the vertices of a regular hexagon of radius rr, let kk be in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. For s∈Ss\in S, define:

ws​(k):=2​(1−cos⁡(2​π​k⋅s)).w_{s}(k):=2\left(1-\cos\left(2\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s\right)\right). (2.22)

The following inequality holds for all vv in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}:

∑s∈Sws​(k)​(s⋅v)2≥14​(∑s∈Sws​(k))​r2​|v|2.\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)\right)r^{2}|v|^{2}. (2.23)

We postpone the proof of Lemma 2.10 to Appendix B, and we explain how to deduce Proposition 2.9.

Proof of Proposition 2.9.

Let 𝐩\mathbf{p} be a N​𝖠2N\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic perturbation and let 𝐩^\widehat{\mathbf{p}} be the Fourier transform of 𝐩\mathbf{p} as in (2.3). We first fix s∈Ss\in S and observe that for all frequencies k∈1N​𝖠^2/𝖠2⋆k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}, we have

𝐩⋅+s^(k)=e−2iπs⋅k𝐩^(k).\widehat{\mathbf{p}_{\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}+s}}(k)=e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k).

Dividing both sides of (2.21) by N2N^{2} and applying Plancherel’s identity (2.4) yields:

1N2∑x′∈𝖠2/N​𝖠2|𝐩x′+s−𝐩x′|2=∑k∈1N​𝖠^2/𝖠2⋆|e−2iπs⋅k−1|2|𝐩^(k)|2,\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+s}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}}\right|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\left|e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}-1\right|^{2}|\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}, (2.24)

as well as (using the fact that s⋅𝐩^​(k)=s⋅𝐩^​(k)\widehat{s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\mathbf{p}}(k)=s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k) because the vector ss is fixed):

1N2∑x′∈𝖠2/N​𝖠2|s⋅(𝐩x′+s−𝐩x′)|2=∑k∈1N​𝖠^2/𝖠2⋆|e−2iπs⋅k−1|2|s⋅𝐩^(k)|2.\frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in\mathsf{A}_{2}/N\mathsf{A}_{2}}\left|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}(\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}+s}-\mathbf{p}_{x^{\prime}})\right|^{2}=\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\left|e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}-1\right|^{2}|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}. (2.25)

Define, as in (2.22), ws(k):=|e−2iπs⋅k−1|2=2(1−cos(2πk⋅s))w_{s}(k):=\left|e^{-2i\pi s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}k}-1\right|^{2}=2\left(1-\cos\left(2\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s\right)\right). Inserting (2.24) and (2.25) into (2.21), the desired inequality becomes:

∑k∈1N​𝖠^2/𝖠2⋆∑s∈Sws​(k)​|s⋅𝐩^​(k)|2≥14​r2​∑k∈1N​𝖠^2/𝖠2⋆(∑s∈Sws​(k))​|𝐩^​(k)|2.\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}r^{2}\sum_{k\in\frac{1}{N}\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}/\mathsf{A}_{2}^{\star}}\left(\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)\right)|\widehat{\mathbf{p}}(k)|^{2}. (2.26)

Then (2.26), and thus (2.21), follows from applying Lemma 2.10 for each frequency kk. ∎

The constant 14\frac{1}{4} appears to be asymptotically sharp as N→∞N\to\infty.

Remark 2.11.

A square is also a spherical 22-design. However, the square lattice ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} - whoses shells are squares - does not satisfy (2.20) for any 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0.

2.8 An auxiliary minimality lemma

Let vv be a fixed unit vector in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}. For all α>0\alpha>0, we consider the function Ψα:ℝ2→[0,+∞)\Psi_{\alpha}:\mathbb{R}^{2}\to[0,+\infty) defined as:

Ψα,v:u↦∑x∈𝖠2|(x+u)⋅v|2​e−πα​|x+u|2\Psi_{\alpha,v}:u\mapsto\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}}|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}} (2.27)

This function is clearly 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}-periodic, so it is enough to study its restriction to the fundamental hexagon ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Proposition 2.12.

Let α†>0\alpha_{\dagger}>0 be fixed. There exists 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 such that for all α∈(0,α†)\alpha\in(0,\alpha_{\dagger}) and for all u∈ℋu\in\mathcal{H}:

Ψα,v​(u)−Ψα,v​(0)≥𝚌​|u|2​e−πα​r⋆2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}. (2.28)

The proof of Proposition 2.12 relies on a cumbersome analysis given in Section C, including a handful of purely numerical inequalities. We emphasize that Ψα,v\Psi_{\alpha,v} is not convex. The value of α†\alpha_{\dagger} is irrelevant at this stage and will be chosen later, our argument works for all fixed α†\alpha_{\dagger} and becomes more difficult for small α\alpha’s.

Remark 2.13.

In the sequel, we will encounter the function:

ω↦∑k∈𝖠^2|(k+ω)⋅v|2​e−πα​|k+ω|2\omega\mapsto\sum_{k\in\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}}|(k+\omega)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|k+\omega|^{2}}

where ω\omega lives in Ω\Omega, the Pontryagin dual of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}. Since the reciprocal lattice 𝖠^2\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2} is obtained from 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} by a rotation and Ω\Omega is obtained from ℋ\mathcal{H} by the same rotation, the conclusions of Proposition 2.12 apply readily.

3 Proof of Theorem 1

In this section, we denote by S⋆S^{\star} the first shell of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}, of sidelength r⋆r_{\star} (see Figure 1), and by 𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}) the “First-Shell” size of a perturbation 𝐩\mathbf{p}, defined as (with Qx\mathrm{Q}_{x} as in (2.5), see also (2.9)):

𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩):=∑x∈S⋆∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qx​(u)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}):=\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u) (3.1)

We also define, with 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}} the matrix-valued spectral measure of 𝐩\mathbf{p} as introduced in Section 2.6:

𝖲𝖬⁡(𝐩):=𝚝𝚛⁡(∫Ω|w|2​𝑑𝖱^​(ω)).\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}):=\mathtt{tr}\left(\int_{\Omega}|w|^{2}\mathtt{d}\widehat{\mathsf{R}}(\omega)\right). (3.2)

By (2.17), if 𝖲𝖬⁡(𝐩)=0\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p})=0 then 𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩)=0\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p})=0. Moreover if 𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩)=0\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p})=0, then clearly 𝐩\mathbf{p} is constant. We prove the following quantitative version of Theorem 1:

Proposition 3.1.

There exists a threshold α†>0\alpha_{\dagger}>0 and a constant 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds. Let 𝐩\mathbf{p} be a periodic perturbation.

  • •

    For α≥α†\alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger}, if ‖𝐩‖≤α−1\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\alpha^{-1}, then:

    Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2)≥𝚌​e−π​α​r⋆2×𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}). (3.3)
  • •

    For 0<α≤α†0<\alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger}, if ‖𝐩‖≤𝚌​e−2​πα​r⋆2\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}, then:

    Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2)≥𝚌​e−πα​r⋆2×𝖲𝖬⁡(𝐩).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}). (3.4)

We divide the proof of Proposition 3.1 in two parts: “α\alpha large” and “α\alpha small”. The first case is easier, we simply use the periodic 22-design inequality of Section 2.7 to get a lower bound on the Hessian of the interaction energy. The second case is more subtle: it requires a distinction between “low” and “high” layers within 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}, and the introduction of the spectral measure 𝖱^\widehat{\mathsf{R}} after having moved to Fourier side thanks to Poisson’s summation formula. The rest of this section is devoted to proving the following two lemmas.

Lemma 3.2 (Large α\alpha).

There exists a threshold α†≥1\alpha_{\dagger}\geq 1, a small constant 𝚌\mathtt{c} and a large constant 𝙲\mathtt{C} such that the following holds for all α≥α†\alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger} and all periodic perturbations 𝐩\mathbf{p}:

  • •

    If ‖𝐩‖≤1α\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}, we have:

    Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2)≥𝚌​e−π​α​r⋆2×𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}). (3.5)
  • •

    Under our general assumption ‖𝐩‖≤r⋆20\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{20}, see (1.3), we have:

Lemma 3.3 (Small α\alpha).

With α†\alpha_{\dagger} as above, there exists a small constant 𝚌\mathtt{c} and a large constant 𝙲\mathtt{C} such that the following holds for all 0<α≤α†0<\alpha\leq\alpha_{\dagger} and all periodic perturbations 𝐩\mathbf{p}:

  • •

    If ‖𝐩‖≤𝚌​e−2​πα​r⋆2\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}, we have:

    Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2)≥𝚌​e−πα​r⋆2×𝖲𝖬⁡(𝐩).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}). (3.7)
  • •

    Under our general assumption ‖𝐩‖≤r⋆20\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{r_{\star}}{20}, see (1.3), we have:

    Eα(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα(𝖠2)≥−𝙲α−1×𝖲𝖬(𝐩).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq-\mathtt{C}\alpha^{-1}\times\mathsf{SM}(\mathbf{p}). (3.8)

The lower bounds (3.6) and (3.8) are not needed for Proposition 3.1 but they follow from the same analysis and will be useful later when considering mixtures of the Φα\Phi_{\alpha}’s in the proof of Theorem 2.

The starting point for both lemmas is (2.6), namely the fact that, with Qx\mathrm{Q}_{x} as in (2.5):

Step 2. A lower bound for the first shell.

We focus on the first shell of the lattice S⋆S^{\star}, of radius r⋆r_{\star}.

Claim 3.4.

There exists 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 such that, if α\alpha is large enough:

∑x∈S⋆∫ℝ2(π​α​|x⋅u|2​e−π​α​|x|2−𝙲​|x|−𝙲−(𝙲+1)​|u|2​e−π​α​|x|2+𝙲​|x|)​𝚍​Qx​(u)≥𝚌​α​e−π​α​r⋆2​𝖥𝖲​(𝐩).\sum_{x\in S^{\star}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\left(\pi\alpha|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}-\mathtt{C}|x|-\mathtt{C}}-(\mathtt{C}+1)|u|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+\mathtt{C}|x|}\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\geq\mathtt{c}\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}). (3.17)
Proof.

Using first Proposition 2.9, then the definition (3.1) of 𝖥𝖲\mathsf{FS}, we have:

(𝚌​α−(𝙲+1)​e𝙲​r⋆)​e−π​α​r⋆2​𝖥𝖲​(𝐩).\left(\mathtt{c}\alpha-(\mathtt{C}+1)e^{\mathtt{C}r_{\star}}\right)e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).

For α\alpha large enough, we have 𝚌​α−(𝙲+1)​e𝙲​r⋆≥12​𝚌​α\mathtt{c}\alpha-(\mathtt{C}+1)e^{\mathtt{C}r_{\star}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\mathtt{c}\alpha, which concludes the proof of Claim 3.4. ∎

This last step only works for a fixed radius of the shell. For “higher” shells, we use a rough lower bound.

Step 3. A lower bound for higher shells.

Combining (3.9), (3.10), (3.12), (3.16), (3.17) and (3.19), and integrating over tt, we find that, for some small constant 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0, provided α\alpha is large enough, the quantity Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) is bounded below by:

(3.20)

We want to argue that, for α\alpha large enough, the second sum in (3.20) is dominated by the first one because of the quickly decreasing Gaussian weight. However, we also need to compare the values of ∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qx​(u)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u) for xx in the first shell, which contribute to 𝖥𝖲⁡(𝐩)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}) (see (3.1)), and its values in “higher” shells.

Step 4. Comparing relative displacements far and close to the origin.
Claim 3.6.

For x∈𝖠2x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}, with |x|>r⋆|x|>r_{\star}, we have:

∫ℝ2|u|2​𝚍​Qx​(u)≤(|x|r⋆)2​𝖥𝖲​(𝐩).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|u|^{2}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{Q}_{x}(u)\leq\left(\frac{|x|}{r_{\star}}\right)^{2}\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}). (3.21)
Proof.

This is easy to see with the probabilistic formulation, for which (see (2.9)):

∎

Step 5. Proof of (3.5).

Inserting (3.21) into (3.20), we find:

Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2)≥2​π​α​(𝚌​α​e−π​α​r⋆2−1r⋆2​∑x∈𝖠2,|x|>r⋆|x|2​e−π​α​|x|2+4​π​|x|)​𝖥𝖲​(𝐩).\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\geq 2\pi\alpha\left(\mathtt{c}\alpha e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}-\frac{1}{r_{\star}^{2}}\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>r_{\star}}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi|x|}\right)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}).

As α→∞\alpha\to\infty, we have ∑x∈𝖠2,|x|>r⋆|x|2​e−π​α​|x|2+4​π​|x|=o⁡(e−π​α​r⋆2)\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2},|x|>r_{\star}}|x|^{2}e^{-\pi\alpha|x|^{2}+4\pi|x|}=o(e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}) which concludes the proof of (3.5) with an extra factor α2\alpha^{2}, which we discard for clarity (here α\alpha is bounded below by 11).

This yields local optimality of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} with respect to Gaussian potentials that are “very peaked”, and are thus essentially nearest-neighbor interactions. The main ingredient is our “periodic 22-design inequality”, which basically leverages the lattice symmetry to ensure that some Hessian is positive.

We conclude the proof of Lemma 3.2 by proving (3.6). We now only assume that ‖𝐩‖\|\mathbf{p}\| satisfies (1.3).

where we used the fact that Qx\mathrm{Q}_{x} is centered, and supported on a disk of radius 2​‖𝐩‖2\|\mathbf{p}\|. We may thus write:

with an error term satisfying:

Combining this with (3.23), (3.24), we write:

using the spectral measures 𝖱^a​b\widehat{\mathsf{R}}^{ab} introduced in Section 2.6. An elementary computation shows that:

3.3 Local optimality for c.m.s.d. functions: proof of Theorem 2

Let ff be a c.m.s.d function and let Wf\mathrm{W}_{f} be the associated measure on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty), such that

f=∫0+∞Φα​𝚍​Wf​(α).f=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\Phi_{\alpha}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha).

In this section, we find conditions on Wf\mathrm{W}_{f} ensuring the existence of ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that for all periodic perturbations 𝐩\mathbf{p}:

If ​‖𝐩‖≤ε​ then ​Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)≥Ef​(𝖠2).\text{If }\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\varepsilon\text{ then }\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\geq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}).

Moreover, we observe that the choice of ε\varepsilon can be done uniformly on certain families of functions ff, as stated in Theorem 2. The starting point is to write:

Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Ef​(𝖠2)=∫0+∞(Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2))​𝚍​Wf​(α),\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2})=\int_{0}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha),

which should be quickly justified: if ff is a c.m.s.d function such that x↦f⁡(|x|)x\mapsto f(|x|) is integrable at infinity (otherwise Ef​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) and Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}) are infinite, see Remark 1.1) then the lim inf\liminf’s defining Ef​(𝖠2),Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}),\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}) in (1.1) are limits, and we simply write:

Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)=limr→∞1|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br|​∑x,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br,x≠y∫0+∞Φα​(|x−y|)​𝚍​Wf​(α)=∫0+∞(limr→∞1|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br|​∑x,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br,x≠yΦα​(|x−y|))​𝚍​Wf​(α).\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}\int_{0}^{+\infty}\Phi_{\alpha}(|x-y|)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\\ =\int_{0}^{+\infty}\left(\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}\Phi_{\alpha}(|x-y|)\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha).

Step 1. Selecting ε\varepsilon for the large α\alpha’s

Let α†\alpha_{\dagger} be the threshold given by Lemma 3.2. We first focus on the contributions coming from α≥α†\alpha\geq\alpha_{\dagger}.

Claim 3.9 (Large α\alpha’s).

Let α1≥α†\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{\dagger} to be chosen later, and assume that ‖𝐩‖≤1α1\|\mathbf{p}\|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha_{1}}. We have:

∫α†+∞(Eα​(𝖠2+𝐩)−Eα​(𝖠2))​𝚍​Wf​(α)≥(𝚌​∫α†+∞e−π​α​r⋆2​𝚍​Wf​(α)−𝙲​∫α1+∞e−π​α2​r⋆2​𝚍​Wf​(α))​𝖥𝖲​(𝐩).\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}\left(\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})-\mathrm{E}_{\alpha}(\mathsf{A}_{2})\right)\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\\ \geq\left(\mathtt{c}\int_{\alpha_{\dagger}}^{+\infty}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)-\mathtt{C}\int_{\alpha_{1}}^{+\infty}e^{-\frac{\pi\alpha}{2}r_{\star}^{2}}\mathtt{d}\mathrm{W}_{f}(\alpha)\right)\mathsf{FS}(\mathbf{p}). (3.49)
Proof.

We split the integral into two parts:

Appendix A Reduction to periodic perturbations: proof of Lemma 2.1

Let ff be a c.m.s.d function - in particular, ff is smooth and decreasing. Without loss of generality, we can assume that x↦f⁡(|x|)x\mapsto f(|x|) (or equivalently r↦r​f​(r)r\mapsto rf(r)) is integrable at ∞\infty, otherwise both Ef​(𝖠2)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}) and Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}) are infinite and there is nothing to prove.

For N≥1N\geq 1, let 𝖫N\mathsf{L}_{N} be the sub-lattice of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} generated by the vectors 2​N​σ2N\sigma and 2​N​τ2N\tau, and let ΛN\Lambda_{N} be a fundamental domain (here a parallelogram) for 𝖫N\mathsf{L}_{N} given by ΛN:={s​N​σ+t​N​τ,(s,t)∈[−1,1]2}\Lambda_{N}:=\left\{sN\sigma+tN\tau,\ (s,t)\in[-1,1]^{2}\right\}.

The sequence of shapes (ΛN)N≥1(\Lambda_{N})_{N\geq 1} converges to ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} in the sense of Van Hove, see [FV17, Sec. 3.2.1]. It is folklore that the following limit exists (see e.g. [BL15, Sec. 2.4]):

limr→∞1|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br|​∑x,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩)∩Br,x≠yf⁡(|x−y|),\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\mathrm{B}_{r},x\neq y}f(|x-y|),

cf. (1.1), and coincides with the same limit taken along the sequence (ΛN)N≥1(\Lambda_{N})_{N\geq 1}, thus we have:

Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)=limN→∞1|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩ΛN|​∑x,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩)∩ΛN,x≠yf⁡(|x−y|).\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N},\ x\neq y}f(|x-y|). (A.1)

In particular, we can take NN large enough such that:

1|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩ΛN|​∑x,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩)∩ΛN,x≠yf⁡(|x−y|)≤Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)+δ.\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N},x\neq y}f(|x-y|)\leq\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})+\delta. (A.2)

We restrict 𝐩\mathbf{p} to the parallelogram ΛN\Lambda_{N}, and define 𝐩per\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}} as the 𝖫N\mathsf{L}_{N}-periodic extension of 𝐩\mathbf{p} to 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}. Of course, we have ‖𝐩per‖≤‖𝐩‖\|\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}}\|\leq\|\mathbf{p}\|. It remains to prove that Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩per)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}}) is not much larger than Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩)\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}).

Consider the sub-sequence of shapes (Λk​N)k≥1(\Lambda_{kN})_{k\geq 1}. For the same reason as above, we have:

Ef​(𝖠2+𝐩per)=limk→∞1|(𝖠2+𝐩per)∩Λk​N|​∑x,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩per)∩Λk​N,x≠yf⁡(|x−y|).\mathrm{E}_{f}(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})=\lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{1}{|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN}|}\sum_{x,y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN},\ x\neq y}f(|x-y|). (A.3)

Notice that Λk​N\Lambda_{kN} is the disjoint union of k2k^{2} disjoint copies of ΛN\Lambda_{N}. Since 𝐩per\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}} is periodic by construction, and coincides with 𝐩\mathbf{p} on ΛN\Lambda_{N}, we have:

|(𝖠2+𝐩per)∩Λk​N|=k2​|(𝖠2+𝐩)∩ΛN|.|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{kN}|=k^{2}|(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p})\cap\Lambda_{N}|.

Moreover, the energy within Λk​N\Lambda_{kN} is given by k2k^{2} times the energy within ΛN\Lambda_{N}, plus the interactions between each copy of ΛN\Lambda_{N} and the rest of the configuration. ∑y∈(𝖠2+𝐩per)∖ΛN|f⁡(x−y)|=odist⁡(x,∂ΛN)→∞​(1),\sum_{y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\setminus\Lambda_{N}}|f(x-y)|=o_{\mathrm{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda_{N})\to\infty}(1),

and thus we can bound the interaction between each copy and the rest of the configuration by:

∑x∈(𝖠2+𝐩per)∩ΛN,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩per)∖ΛN|f⁡(|x−y|)|=o⁡(|ΛN|),\sum_{x\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{N},y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\setminus\Lambda_{N}}\left|f(|x-y|)\right|=o\left(|\Lambda_{N}|\right),

1|ΛN|​∑x∈(𝖠2+𝐩per)∩ΛN,y∈(𝖠2+𝐩per)∖ΛN|f⁡(x−y)|≤δ,\frac{1}{|\Lambda_{N}|}\sum_{x\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\cap\Lambda_{N},y\in(\mathsf{A}_{2}+\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{per}})\setminus\Lambda_{N}}|f(x-y)|\leq\delta,

Appendix B Proof of the “geometric” Lemma 2.10

Without loss of generality, we assume that SS has sidelength r=1r=1. For k,vk,v fixed, we want to prove:

∑s∈Sws​(k)​|s⋅v|2≥14​(∑s∈Sws​(k))​|v|2, with ​ws​(k):=2​(1−cos⁡(2​π​k⋅s)).\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}\geq\frac{1}{4}\left(\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(k)\right)|v|^{2},\quad\text{ with }w_{s}(k):=2\left(1-\cos\left(2\pi k\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s\right)\right).

together with their opposites, which yield the same contributions. We obtain:

M=1w1+w2+w3​(w1+w2+w3434​(w2−w3)34​(w2−w3)34​(w2+w3))\mathrm{M}=\frac{1}{w_{1}+w_{2}+w_{3}}\begin{pmatrix}w_{1}+\tfrac{w_{2}+w_{3}}{4}&\tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(w_{2}-w_{3})\\[2.84526pt] \tfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(w_{2}-w_{3})&\tfrac{3}{4}(w_{2}+w_{3})\end{pmatrix}

where we write w1,w2,w3w_{1},w_{2},w_{3} instead of ws1​(k),ws2​(k),ws3​(k)w_{s_{1}}(k),w_{s_{2}}(k),w_{s_{3}}(k). Clearly, 𝚝𝚛​M=1\mathtt{tr}\mathrm{M}=1, and detM\det\mathrm{M} is given by

Proving that λmin≥14\lambda_{\min}\geq\frac{1}{4} will imply (B.1). By our expression (B.2) for detM\det\mathrm{M}, this is equivalent to having:

wj=2​(1−cj)=4​sin2⁡(θj2).w_{j}=2\left(1-c_{j}\right)=4\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{j}}{2}\right).

The inequality (B.4) can then be re-written, after some algebra, as:

4​(c1​c2+c2​c3+c3​c1)−(c1+c2+c3)2−2​(c1+c2+c3)+3≥0.4\left(c_{1}c_{2}+c_{2}c_{3}+c_{3}c_{1}\right)-\left(c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}\right)^{2}-2\left(c_{1}+c_{2}+c_{3}\right)+3\geq 0. (B.5)

The inequality (B.5) expresses that the right-hand side of (B.6) is non-negative, and is thus equivalent to:

16​sin2⁡(θ12)​sin2⁡(θ22)−16​sin2⁡(θ12)​sin2⁡(θ22)​cos2⁡(θ1−θ22)≥0,16\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\right)\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}\right)-16\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\right)\sin^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{2}}{2}\right)\cos^{2}\left(\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{2}\right)\geq 0,

which is true, and concludes the proof of the claim. ∎

Now, the inequality (B.4) being satisfied, we get (B.1), which yields the result.

Recall that vv is a fixed unit vector and that Ψα,v\Psi_{\alpha,v} is defined on the fundamental domain ℋ\mathcal{H} of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2} by:

r⋆=23≈1.0746,α¯:=0.552.r_{\star}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}}\approx 1.0746,\quad\bar{\alpha}:=0.552.

Assume that α∈(α¯,α†)\alpha\in(\bar{\alpha},\alpha_{\dagger}) and fix a unit vector vv.

with non-negative weights ws​(u)=2​(1−cos⁡(2​π​u⋅s))w_{s}(u)=2\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right) as in (2.22). Applying Lemma 2.10 we get:

π​α​∑s∈Sws​(u)​|s⋅v|2−12​∑s∈Sws​(u)≥(14​π​α​r2−12)​∑s∈Sws​(u)=14​π​r2​(α−2π​r2)​∑s∈Sws​(u).\pi\alpha\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)\geq\left(\frac{1}{4}\pi\alpha r^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\right)\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u)=\frac{1}{4}\pi r^{2}\left(\alpha-\frac{2}{\pi r^{2}}\right)\sum_{s\in S}w_{s}(u). Since r≥r⋆r\geq r_{\star}, since we assume α≥α¯\alpha\geq\bar{\alpha}, and since the following numerical inequality is true:

the right-hand side of (C.6) is non-negative, thus so is (C.5).

All the shells have a positive contribution, we focus on the first one.

Claim C.2.

For all u∈ℋu\in\mathcal{H}, we have, S⋆S^{\star} being the first shell of the lattice 𝖠^2\widehat{\mathsf{A}}_{2}:

By the choice of the fundamental cell ℋ\mathcal{H}, we have |u⋅s|≤12|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s|\leq\frac{1}{2} for all s∈S⋆s\in S^{\star} and u∈ℋu\in\mathcal{H}. Using the lower bound 1−cos⁡x≥2π2​x21-\cos x\geq\frac{2}{\pi^{2}}x^{2} valid for |x|≤π|x|\leq\pi, we get:

ws​(u)=2​(1−cos⁡(2​π​u⋅s))≥16​|u⋅s|2.w_{s}(u)=2\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right)\geq 16|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s|^{2}.

Combining (C.5), (C.6) and (C.8) we obtain:

∑s∈S⋆(2​π​α​|s⋅v|2−1)​e−π​α​|s|2​(1−cos⁡(2​π​u⋅s))≥12​π​r⋆4​(α−2π​r⋆2)​|u|2.\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}\left(2\pi\alpha|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}-1\right)e^{-\pi\alpha|s|^{2}}\left(1-\cos(2\pi u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}s)\right)\geq 12\pi r_{\star}^{4}\left(\alpha-\frac{2}{\pi r_{\star}^{2}}\right)|u|^{2}. Ψα,v​(u)−Ψα,v​(0)≥𝚌​α3​e−π​α​r⋆2​|u|2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}\alpha^{3}e^{-\pi\alpha r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}.

C.2 Second case: α\alpha small.

Returning to the original expression (C.1) for Ψα,v\Psi_{\alpha,v}, we write for u∈ℋu\in\mathcal{H}:

Ψα,v​(u)=|u⋅v|2​e−πα​|u|2+∑x∈𝖠2∖{0}|(x+u)⋅v|2​e−πα​|x+u|2,Ψα,v​(0)=∑x∈𝖠2∖{0}|x⋅v|2​e−πα​|x|2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)=|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}+\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}}|(x+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x+u|^{2}},\quad\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)=\sum_{x\in\mathsf{A}_{2}\setminus\{0\}}|x\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|x|^{2}}. (C.10)

Until the end of the proof, we assume that α\alpha is “small” in the sense:

α≤α¯:=0.552\alpha\leq\bar{\alpha}:=0.552 (C.11)

and our goal is to prove, for some constant 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 independent of α,u\alpha,u:

Ψα,v​(u)−Ψα,v​(0)≥𝚌​e−πα​r⋆2​|u|2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}|u|^{2}. (C.12)

The proof uses only elementary tools but is a bit intricate. We treat the first shell (and the origin) and the higher shells separately, and then distinguish several regimes in each case.

C.3 The first shell and the origin

Let S⋆S^{\star} be the first shell of 𝖠2\mathsf{A}_{2}. We denote by Ψα,v⋆\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star} the contribution coming from S⋆∪{0}S^{\star}\cup\{0\}:

Ψα,v⋆:u↦|u⋅v|2​e−πα​|u|2+∑s∈S⋆|(s+u)⋅v|2​e−πα​|s+u|2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}:u\mapsto|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}+\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}.

Using the 22-design property (2.18), for every shell SS of radius rr we have

∑s∈S|s⋅v|2​e−πα​|s|2=3​r2​e−πα​r2,\sum_{s\in S}|s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s|^{2}}=3r^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r^{2}},

so we are interested in finding a lower bound of the form:

Ψα,v⋆​(u)−Ψα,v⋆​(0)=|u⋅v|2​e−πα​|u|2+∑s∈S⋆|(s+u)⋅v|2​e−πα​|s+u|2−3​r⋆2​e−πα​r⋆2≥𝚌​|u|2​e−πα​r⋆2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)=|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}+\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}. (C.13)

We will consider three cases:

  1. 1.

    If |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “large”, a direct computation suffices.

  2. 2.

    If |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “small” and |u||u| is “small”, we use a Taylor expansion.

  3. 3.

    If |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “small” and |u||u| is “large”, direct or perturbative computations fail. We identify a “good vertex” within the first shell and show that its contribution is always big enough for (C.12) to hold. This relies on a tedious identification of the “worst case scenario” among all possible parameters.

Some of the arguments below rely on purely numerical inequalities between certain explicit quantities. A Python notebook that checks those inequalities is available here.

C.4 First situation: |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is large.

This first part deals only with the contribution of the origin. We make a simple observation:

Claim C.3 (If |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is “large”.).

There exists a constant 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds. Assume that u,α,vu,\alpha,v are such that:

|u⋅v|≥3.01​r⋆​eπ2​α​(|u|2−r⋆2),|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\geq\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)}, (C.14)

then we have:

Ψα,v⋆​(u)−Ψα,v⋆​(0)≥𝚌​|u|2​e−πα​r⋆2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}. (C.15)
Proof.

Discarding the contribution from the first shell and keeping only the one from 00 in (C.13), we get:

Ψα,v⋆​(u)−Ψα,v⋆​(0)≥|u⋅v|2​e−πα​|u|2−3​r⋆2​e−πα​r⋆2=(|u⋅v|2​eπα​(r⋆2−|u|2)−3​r⋆2)​e−πα​r⋆2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}=\left(|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(r_{\star}^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)}-3r_{\star}^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.

Our assumption (C.14) ensures that

|u⋅v|2​eπα​(r⋆2−|u|2)≥3.01​r⋆2,|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{\frac{\pi}{\alpha}\left(r_{\star}^{2}-|u|^{2}\right)}\geq 3.01r_{\star}^{2},

so in particular, for some small constant 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 we can guarantee that, as stated in (C.15):

Ψα,v⋆​(u)−Ψα,v⋆​(0)≥𝚌​r⋆2​e−πα​r⋆2≥𝚌​|u|2​e−πα​r⋆2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}r_{\star}^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}.

∎

In the sequel, when considering Ψα,v⋆\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}, we may thus assume that |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is not “large” as in (C.14).

C.5 Second situation: |u⋅v||u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v| is small and |u||u| is small.

We now turn to the case where |u||u| is small compared to α\alpha, in the sense that πα​|u|≤μ⋆\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\leq\mu_{\star}, for a certain threshold μ⋆\mu_{\star}.

Lemma C.4.

There exists 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds. Assume that u,v,αu,v,\alpha are such that:

α≤α¯,|u⋅v|≤3.01​r⋆​eπ2​α​(|u|2−r⋆2),πα​|u|≤μ⋆=2.73.\alpha\leq\bar{\alpha},\quad|u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|\leq\sqrt{3.01}r_{\star}e^{\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\left(|u|^{2}-r_{\star}^{2}\right)},\quad\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|\leq\mu_{\star}=2.73. (C.16)

Then we have:

Ψα,v⋆​(u)−Ψα,v⋆​(0)≥𝚌​|u|2​e−πα​r⋆2.\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(u)-\Psi_{\alpha,v}^{\star}(0)\geq\mathtt{c}|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}. (C.17)
Proof.

We will prove that

∑s∈S⋆|(s+u)⋅v|2​e−πα​|s+u|2−3​r⋆2≥0.01​|u|2​e−πα​r⋆2,\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}|(s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}-3r_{\star}^{2}\geq 0.01|u|^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}, (C.18)

which clearly implies (C.17). Expand the squares in the summands of (C.18) and write, for s∈S⋆s\in S^{\star}:

((s+u)⋅v)2e−πα​|s+u|2=((s⋅v)2+2(s⋅v)(u⋅v)+(u⋅v)2)e−2​παs⋅ue−πα​|u|2−πα​r⋆2.((s+u)\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|s+u|^{2}}=\left((s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}+2(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)+(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}e^{-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}|u|^{2}-\frac{\pi}{\alpha}r_{\star}^{2}}. (C.19)

We focus first on the ss-dependent part of the sum, namely:

𝖲𝗎𝗆:=∑s∈S⋆((s⋅v)2+2(s⋅v)(u⋅v)+(u⋅v)2)e−2​παs⋅u.\mathsf{Sum}:=\sum_{s\in S^{\star}}\left((s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}+2(s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)+(u\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}v)^{2}\right)e^{-\frac{2\pi}{\alpha}s\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}u}. (C.20)

Step 1. A Taylor expansion to third order.

Using the following elementary lower bound:

There exists a constant 𝚌>0\mathtt{c}>0 such that the following holds. Assume that u,α,vu,\alpha,v are such that:

Studying the full sum over the six vertices is challenging, but fortunately we can show that the contribution of a single “good” vertex of S⋆S^{\star} is sufficient to beat the negative term.

Step 2. Worst case for α\alpha.
Claim C.7.

For all admissible u,αu,\alpha, we have:

G⁡(u,α)≥G⁡(u,αm​(ρ)),αm​(ρ):=min⁡(α¯,π​ρμ⋆).\mathrm{G}(u,\alpha)\geq\mathrm{G}\left(u,\alpha_{m}(\rho)\right),\quad\alpha_{m}(\rho):=\min\left(\bar{\alpha},\ \frac{\pi\rho}{\mu_{\star}}\right). (C.32)

It follows from the fact that the map α↦G⁡(u,α)\alpha\mapsto\mathrm{G}(u,\alpha) is decreasing. Indeed:

ϕ:=π3−θ∈[π6,π3],δ⁡(ρ):=arcsin⁡(κ⁡(ρ))\phi:=\frac{\pi}{3}-\theta\in\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{\pi}{3}\right],\quad\delta(\rho):=\arcsin\left(\kappa(\rho)\right)

H:(ρ,ϕ)↦N​(ρ,ϕ)2​exp⁡(παm​(ρ)​(2​r⋆​ρ​cos⁡ϕ−ρ2)).\mathrm{H}:(\rho,\phi)\mapsto\mathrm{N}(\rho,\phi)^{2}\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{\alpha_{m}(\rho)}\left(2r_{\star}\rho\cos\phi-\rho^{2}\right)\right).
Step 5. Worst case for ϕ\phi.
Claim C.10.

For all admissible ρ\rho, the quantity H⁡(ρ,ϕ)\mathrm{H}(\rho,\phi) is minimal at ϕ=π3\phi=\frac{\pi}{3}.

Proof.

The proof goes in two steps: first, we show that the minimum is always at π3\frac{\pi}{3} or π6\frac{\pi}{6}, then we compare the two values directly and find that the smaller one is always at π3\frac{\pi}{3}.

1. The minimum is at the endpoints. It suffices to show that ∂ϕH⁡(ρ,⋅)\partial_{\phi}\mathrm{H}(\rho,\mathbin{\vbox{\hbox{\scalebox{1.3}{$\cdot$}}}}) is decreasing for fixed ρ\rho. Write:

We split the discussion into several cases.

  • •

and we are left to prove that the ratio N⁡(ρ,π6)N⁡(ρ,π3)\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})} cannot be too small, so that:

(N⁡(ρ,π6)N⁡(ρ,π3))2​exp⁡(μ⋆​r⋆​(3−1))≥1.\left(\frac{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{6})}{\mathrm{N}(\rho,\frac{\pi}{3})}\right)^{2}\exp\left(\mu_{\star}r_{\star}\left(\sqrt{3}-1\right)\right)\geq 1.

    If 0≤ρ≤9​r⋆200\leq\rho\leq\frac{9r_{\star}}{20}. Then of course ρ≤12​r⋆\rho\leq\frac{1}{2}r_{\star}. According to the expressions for N\mathrm{N} given in (C.38), we have:

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
